# NotifJournal

A private, on-device notification journal for a single personal Android phone.

NotifJournal is a Kotlin / Jetpack Compose app that listens to your
notifications via Android's `NotificationListenerService`, immediately
persists them into a local Room database, and reliably syncs structured
records to your own Firebase project. It is the replacement for the
MacroDroid workflow you used to run for this job.

The app is built around two halves: a **private capture engine** that
records notifications via the system `NotificationListenerService`, and
a **GUI control plane** that lets you decide what gets captured, how
it's parsed, where it ends up, and how the sync behaves.

---

## GUI and Settings Control Plane

The control plane is the polished, Apple-style settings layer that sits
on top of the capture engine. It is composed of a bottom navigation
shell and seven top-level screens, all built with the same reusable
components.

### Bottom navigation

The app shell exposes five destinations:

| Tab | Path | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dashboard** | `screens/dashboard/` | At-a-glance summary, sync health, capture state, action cards. |
| **Apps** | `screens/apps/` | Pick which apps feed the journal; allowlist, denylist, system apps. |
| **Parser** | `screens/parser/` | Visual rule editor with live preview, no JSON editing. |
| **Backend** | `screens/backend/` | Choose Firestore / Frappe / SuiteCRM / Custom API / Local only. |
| **Settings** | `screens/settings/` | Identity, theme, retention, dedupe, kill switch, data ops. |

Two auxiliary screens are reachable from the Dashboard:

- **Address / Lead Mapping** (`screens/mapping/`) — preview parsed addresses, set dedup strategy.
- **Diagnostics** (`screens/diagnostics/`) — listener, queue, crashes, log export.

### Reusable components

Everything in the control plane is built from a small set of
single-purpose composables in `ui/components/`:

| Component | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `AppScaffold` | Edge-to-edge scaffold with large display-style header, optional bottom bar. |
| `PremiumCard` | 20 dp rounded card with soft shadow, the default container. |
| `SettingsSection` | Grouped-list "Apple settings" card with a header and rows. |
| `SettingRow` | Tappable row with leading icon chip, label, supporting text, trailing control. |
| `LargeIconButton` | 96 dp touch target for the dashboard action grid. |
| `StatusPill` | Color-coded status chip (OK / WARN / ERROR / INFO / NEUTRAL). |
| `EmptyState` | Centered icon + title + description + action. |
| `SearchablePickerSheet` | Modal bottom sheet with debounced search and selectable list. |
| `MultiSelectAppPicker` | Searchable, multi-select list of installed apps with icons. |
| `ParserRuleEditor` | Inline editor for one parser rule, with live preview against sample input. |
| `SyncHealthCard` | 0–100 health card with progress bar, status pill, and three quick stats. |

### Screens

#### 1. Dashboard

The landing tab. Renders a hero card summarising the capture state,
four metric cards (Pending, Failed, Selected apps, Last alert), the
`SyncHealthCard`, and a 2×2 grid of `LargeIconButton`s for quick
navigation.

Key behaviours:

- The hero card reads the current access state from the
  `NotificationAccessChecker` and the paused state from the
  `AppFilterRepository`. It recomputes on every relevant flow tick.
- The "Last alert" metric links to the Feed screen.
- "Apps", "Parser", "Backend", "Onboarding", and "Settings" action
  cards navigate to the corresponding top-level destination.
- The "Kill switch" action opens Settings; the actual switch lives
  in `Settings → Capture → Capture paused`.

![Dashboard placeholder](docs/dashboard.png)

> **Note:** The PNGs in this README are placeholders. Run the
> app on a phone and screenshot each screen; the layout matches
> the descriptions below exactly.

#### 2. App Selection

Three modes in the top card:

- **Capture all** (default) — every notification is recorded.
- **Allowlist** — only the packages you select.
- **Denylist** — every app except the packages you select.

Below the mode picker is the `MultiSelectAppPicker`:

- A search field (matches app name or package name, case-insensitive).
- A "Show system apps" toggle.
- A "X selected" counter and a Select all / Clear all button.
- A list of apps with their real icon, app name, and package name.

content.text:
- A list of apps with their real icon, app name, and package name.
- Bulk add / remove flows through `SettingsRepository.setFilterPackages`.

The `SettingsRepository` stores the mode in a DataStore string and
the package set as a string set, with a 60-second debounce on the
in-memory snapshot for the listener service.

#### 3. Parser Settings

A visual rule editor. The screen lists existing rules in order with
per-row toggle / duplicate / delete / move-up / move-down actions.
Tap a rule to edit it, or tap "New rule" to create one.

The editor (`ParserRuleEditor`) renders:

- **Source app** — pick from a list or leave as "Any" to apply to every package.
- **Notification field** — pick from `title`, `text`, `bigText`, `subText`, `summaryText`, `tickerText`, `packageName`.
- **Extraction method** — pick from the full list:

  | Method | Description |
  | --- | --- |
  | Contains | Match if the field contains the pattern (case-insensitive). |
  | Starts with | Match if the field starts with the pattern. |
  | Ends with | Match if the field ends with the pattern. |
  | Regex | First capture group is returned, falling back to full match. |
  | Split before | Return the text after the first match of the pattern. |
  | Split after | Return the text after the first match of the pattern. |
  | Text between | Pattern is two strings separated by `|`. |
  | Address detector | Built-in US-address detector; pattern ignored. |
  | Phone detector | Built-in US phone-number detector; pattern ignored. |
  | Email detector | Built-in email detector; pattern ignored. |

- **Pattern** — free-text, with method-specific placeholder + helper text.
- **Output field** — name of the field that the extracted value is stored under.
- **Rule enabled** switch.
- **Live preview** — type a sample into the preview input, the
  editor runs the rule against it and shows the output, no match, or
  the rule error inline.

> **Why no JSON?** The previous build had a JSON config screen; it
> was replaced with this visual builder so Tony can iterate without
> context-switching to a text editor. The rules are still stored as
> structured rows in the `parser_rules` Room table; nothing is lost.

The rules are persisted in the new `parser_rules` Room table with a
unique-by-id primary key, an `orderIndex` for ordering, and an
`enabled` flag. The `ParserEngine` reads them at apply time and
caches them in-memory, invalidating on save.

#### 4. Address / Lead Mapping

A read-only preview screen that runs the active parser rules against
the last 100 captured notifications and surfaces anything that
matched a `leadAddress`, `phoneNumber`, or `email` output field.

Three dedup strategies for the future CRM write:

- **Create new** — always create a new lead.
- **Update existing** — update the matching lead with the new fields.
- **Activity only** — log a CRM activity, do not create or update the lead.

#### 5. Sync / Backend Settings

The Backend screen lets you pick where the captured records end up.
Five modes are supported:

| Mode | Where records go | Auth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Firestore** | `users/{uid}/devices/{deviceId}/notifications/{eventId}` | Anonymous Firebase Auth (handled by `FirebaseAuthRepository`) |
| **Frappe CRM** | `POST {base}/api/resource/Notification Journal` | Frappe `token {apiKey}:{apiSecret}` header |
| **SuiteCRM** | `POST {base}/Api/V8/module` | OAuth2 Bearer token |
| **Custom API** | `POST {endpoint}` | `Authorization: Bearer {token}` |
| **Local only** | nowhere — Room is the canonical store | n/a |

The endpoint URL is a plain field. The auth token / API key is
written to a `MasterKey`-backed `EncryptedSharedPreferences` so
it's encrypted at rest with the Android Keystore as the source of
truth. **Only the active provider's key is kept** — switching
providers does not auto-clear the previous one (use the in-app
"clear" button to scrub).

Retry settings (3 sliders):

- **Retries** — how many times WorkManager retries a failed batch (1–10).
- **Backoff** — exponential backoff start, in seconds (10–300).
- **Timeout** — per-request timeout, in seconds (5–120).

The "Test connection" button runs `Backend.testConnection()` on a
background coroutine and reports latency, status code, or error
message inline.

#### 6. Diagnostics

The Diagnostics screen is the on-device health-check. It renders:

- **Device** card — manufacturer, model, Android version, app version.
- **Queue** card — pending, failed, total (last 100), last error.
- **Maintenance** card — Export logs, Clear logs, Reset local queue.
- **Recent log lines** — the last 500 log entries from
  `DiagnosticLogStore`, ordered newest first.

#### 7. Settings

The Settings screen is the system's "preferences" pane. Sections:

| Section | Rows |
| --- | --- |
| **Identity** | Firebase sign-in (anonymous by default), Permission checklist link. |
| **Capture** | Kill switch (pause / resume), Local retention (7/30/90/180/365 days or Forever). |
| **Dedupe** | Toggle the dedupe window. |
| **Appearance** | Theme: System / Light / Dark. |
| **Data** | Delete all local data, Record a test crash. |

### Strongly-typed settings

Everything is stored in strongly-typed data classes, not JSON:

- `AppFilterSettings` — mode + package set (DataStore).
- `ParserRule` — Room row with a typed `ParserField` and `ExtractionMethod` enum.
- `BackendConfig` — single Room row, every field a typed value.
- `AddressMapping` — Room table reserved for future geocoder integration.
- `DedupeSettings`, `RetentionPeriod`, `ThemeMode`, `LeadDedupStrategy`, `GeocodingProvider` — Kotlin enums + value classes.

The schema migration `MIGRATION_1_2` adds the new tables without
touching the existing `notifications` table. Old local records are
preserved on upgrade.

### Preview annotations

Every top-level screen has a `@Preview` annotation with a
`@PreviewParameter` provider that renders both the "everything is
healthy" and "action needed" variants. Designers can iterate on the
look-and-feel without running the app.

### Compose UI tests

The repo includes unit tests for the parser engine, dedup keys,
extraction methods, and the Room DAO. Compose UI tests live in
`src/androidTest/java/com/tony/notifjournal/ui/` and can be run with:

```bash
./gradlew :app:connectedDebugAndroidTest
```

A smoke test exercises the app picker, the parser rule editor, the
backend type selector, and the connection-state pill. The tests
require a real device or emulator because the `androidx.compose.ui:ui-test`
manifest setup uses the platform `ComposeTestRule`.

---

This is **not** a stealth, hidden, or rooted app. The listener only
runs after you explicitly grant Notification Access in System
Settings, the app is visible in the launcher, and every captured
record stays in plain text on the device for you to audit.

---

## Values Tony Must Provide

The project will not build a working APK without these. The
`google-services.json` placeholder is included but contains obvious
fake values — replace it before installing the app.

| What | Where | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `app/google-services.json` | Firebase console → Project Settings → Your apps → Android app → "google-services.json" | Required by the `com.google.gms.google-services` Gradle plugin. |
| Firebase project ID | Same file | Becomes the namespace for `users/{userId}/...` in Firestore. |
| Web API key | Same file | Used by the Firebase Android SDK for auth. |
| `local.properties` (optional) | Project root | `sdk.dir=/path/to/Android/sdk` for command-line builds. |
| `keystore.properties` (optional) | Project root | If you want a signed release APK, point Gradle at your own keystore. |
| App Check provider (optional) | Build config | The default is **off** because Play Integrity is unreliable on sideloaded builds. Enable in `AppContainer` if you ship a Play Store build. |

Nothing in this list is recoverable from a public source. Firebase
client configuration is *not* a secret — anyone with it can identify
the project, but only an authenticated user can read or write
records. Security is enforced by Firestore rules, not by hiding the
config.

---

Plenty to unpack here. Let me handle it in the order you asked, then zoom out because the new direction actually changes the Firebase question.

## Firebase project setup

**Name doesn't matter functionally** — it's just a display label in the console. Use whatever reads clean to you (`nfa-alerts`, `notif-journal`, `tony-notifs`, etc.). The only thing that has to match a specific string is the **Android package name** in Firebase, which is `com.tony.notifjournal` per the repo's `app/build.gradle.kts` — Firebase keys it off that, and it has to match exactly or the Android app's auth fails.

**What else you need at setup time:**

| Field | Where to get it |
| --- | --- |
| Project ID | Auto-generated, you can edit it. Becomes the Firestore namespace and is baked into `google-services.json`. |
| `google-services.json` | Project Settings → Your apps → Android → Download. Drops into `app/google-services.json`. |
| Web API key | Same file. Used by the Firebase Android SDK for auth. |
| Region for Firestore | Pick at DB creation time — closest to you, can't be changed later without a re-import. |

**One important thing to flag — re-think whether you need Firebase at all** under the new flow.

## Zoom out: does the new architecture even need Firestore?

The current stack is:

> BNN notifications → Android listener → Room (local) → **Firestore (cloud)** → nfa-alerts PWA reads Firestore

If the new flow is "everything local, alerts end up on this PC and the nfa-alerts PWA reads from there" — Firestore is a round-trip you don't need. It adds a cloud dependency, an auth layer, and a billing surface for no reason.

The new topology I'd suggest is:

> BNN notifications → Android listener → Room (local) → **HTTP POST to a small local server on this PC** → **local DB on this PC** → nfa-alerts PWA reads from that same local DB

The good news: **the Android app already supports this**. Look at the Backend tab options — there's a "Custom API" mode that does exactly `POST {endpoint}` with a bearer token, retry sliders, and the "Test connection" button. You don't need to rebuild the app, you just point that endpoint at `http://<this-pc's-LAN-ip>:PORT/api/notifications` and you're done.

So the real questions are:

1. **What runs on the PC to receive the POSTs?** A small Node/Python/Go service writing to SQLite or Postgres.
2. **How does the nfa-alerts PWA read from that DB?** Either a thin HTTP API in front of the local DB, or a direct SQLite read if both run on the same machine.
3. **Is your phone always on the same Wi-Fi as the PC?** If not, you need either a tunnel (Tailscale, Cloudflare Tunnel) or to keep a cloud relay as fallback.

I'd recommend: **SQLite + a 200-line Fastify/Express server on the PC, accessed by both the Android app and the nfa-alerts PWA over the LAN.** SQLite because it's a single-file DB, no service to manage, perfect for a personal journaling workload.

So: **skip Firebase entirely** for the new flow. Build the small PC server, point the Android app at it via Custom API mode, and rewire nfa-alerts to read from the same local server.

## Flutter vs React Native

Honest comparison, no hype:

| | **Flutter** | **React Native** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Language | Dart (new for you) | JavaScript / TypeScript (you already know this from Next.js) |
| UI rendering | Skia — draws its own pixels, identical look on every platform | Native widgets (or fabric) — looks "native" but varies per platform |
| Web target | Yes (CanvasKit, heavier) | Yes (react-native-web, mature) |
| Code reuse from Next.js | **Low** — have to rewrite in Dart, business logic ported by hand | **High** — keep React, hooks, state, types, API clients, validation logic |
| Performance | Slightly better, especially for animations | Excellent, the gap is mostly gone post-Fabric/Hermes |
| Tooling / hot reload | Excellent | Excellent |
| Native module story | Platform channels (a bit verbose) | Native modules + huge ecosystem |
| Single team velocity | One language across mobile/web/desktop | Same JS/TS you've already got |
| Bundle / startup on web | Heavy first load (CanvasKit WASM) | Lighter, ships actual web components |

**My recommendation: React Native**, specifically because you're porting from a Next.js codebase. The mental model stays React — components, hooks, state, routing patterns transfer 1:1. You reuse the business logic, the types, the API client, the validation, the data shapes. The UI layer is the only real rewrite, and even there you can use `react-native-web` to keep the same components running on the PWA.

Flutter is the right call if you want one consistent UI across all platforms regardless of OS conventions, or if you're starting from scratch with no existing code. Neither applies here.

## AI tools that can read the live Next.js code and plan the conversion

Honest answer — **none of them will do a one-click full conversion**. What they can do is the planning + bulk of the boilerplate:

| Tool | Best for | Why I'd reach for it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cursor** | Reading the live Next.js repo, asking "convert this file to RN", accepting the diff inline | Best DX for "I have a live codebase, port it" |
| **Claude Code / GPT with codebase indexing** | Architectural mapping, identifying what doesn't translate (Next.js API routes, getServerSideProps, file routing) | Strongest at the "what changes" planning pass |
| **Cody (Sourcegraph)** | Same as Cursor but better at huge monorepos | If nfa-alerts is big |
| **v0.dev** | Generating the new UI components one at a time | Useful for the UI layer rewrite, prompts like "make a notification card like this" |
| **DhiWise** | Has explicit Next.js → React Native scaffolding | Niche, but real |
| **bolt.new / Lovable** | Spinning up a fresh RN/Expo project quickly | Good for the new repo shell |

**Practical workflow I'd actually run:**

1. Hand Cursor (or me, with codebase access) the nfa-alerts repo.
2. Get a mapping doc: which Next.js files become which React Native files, which Next.js-specific concepts need rewriting.
3. Scaffold a fresh **Expo** (managed RN) project — Expo is the modern RN path, handles iOS/Android/web from one config.
4. Migrate in layers: types → API client → state/store → components → screens → navigation.
5. Use `react-native-web` so the PWA keeps working the whole time you port.

## Values You Must Provide

For the new architecture, before I can build anything:

| What | Format | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Where should Android write to?** Confirm the plan: a local HTTP server on this PC, endpoint like `http://192.168.x.x:PORT/api/notifications` | URL + port | Drives the Android app's Custom API config |
| **PC server stack preference** | Node (Express/Fastify) / Python (FastAPI) / Go / something else | I default to **Node + Fastify + better-sqlite3** for "small + zero-config", but you may have a stack preference |
| **Phone-to-PC reachability** | Always on same LAN? Need a tunnel? | If not always on LAN, we need Tailscale / Cloudflare Tunnel as a relay |
| **nfa-alerts codebase** | Repo URL or path on this machine so I can read it | I need to see the actual code to plan the port — every Next.js app is different |
| **Rename the Android app?** | e.g. `com.tony.nfa-alerts` instead of `com.tony.notifjournal` | If we're keeping the Android capture app, do we want the package to reflect nfa-alerts? |
| **Keep Notification Access flow** | yes / no | The whole "grant notification access in System Settings" onboarding stays the same |

For the Firebase question specifically — **if you skip it, you don't need to create the project at all**. If you want to keep it as a fallback / for the auth flow, then create it with package name `com.tony.notifjournal` and download `google-services.json`. But my strong recommendation is: **don't bother creating the Firebase project for this new direction** — it adds a dependency you don't need.

Want me to read the nfa-alerts codebase next? Point me at the repo path and I'll map out the Next.js → React Native port concretely, file by file. And tell me your stack preference for the PC server and I'll sketch the API + DB schema for the new local backend.

Read the README, looked at the monorepo, and pulled up that `google-services.json`. Before we plan a thing, **I need to push back on the "all local" framing** — for the commercial app it doesn't work, and pushing through it will burn a lot of time and money. Then I'll lay out what I think you actually want.

## Why "all local" breaks the chaser/supe app

You said two things that contradict each other. Let me name them:

1. **"All be local"** — capture → PC → nfa-alerts reads from PC
2. **"Half the day I'm away from the PC"** — your home PC is offline ~12 hours

The chaser and supe apps need **24/7 real-time fire alerts in the field**. They're remote employees responding to incidents, not sitting on your couch. If the canonical server is a PC at your house, they lose alerts the moment you leave. And a home PC is a single point of failure for a US-wide commercial service — power blip, ISP hiccup, Windows update, you sleep, your chasers sleep too.

The screenshots also tell me this is a real multi-user product: separate Chaser and Supe apps, live chat between roles, location sharing, push notifications when alerts come in. None of that survives "all local."

**The right mental model:**

| What | Where it should live |
| --- | --- |
| Your personal BNN capture phone (the `notification-database` app) | Sends to the cloud, not your home PC |
| Canonical alert store | Cloud (managed Postgres or Firestore) |
| nfa-alerts chaser/supe apps | Read from cloud over WebSocket / FCM |
| CMS back office | Cloud web app |
| Marketing site + SEO | Cloud (Vercel, fine) |
| **Your home PC** | Just a viewer / dashboard for you when you're at home, optional |

The `notification-database` Android app is your **personal capture device** (replaces MacroDroid on your phone). It has nothing to do with serving the commercial app. Don't conflate them.

## What to keep, what to drop

You're already running on Firebase for Auth, Firestore, FCM. **Don't rip that out.** It's solving real problems:

| Firebase service | Why it earns its keep |
| --- | --- |
| **Firebase Auth** | User sign-in for chasers, supes, admins. Phone + email + password. Already integrated. |
| **Firestore** | Real-time document sync — drives the live alert feed and chat. Real-time without you writing WebSocket code. |
| **FCM (Cloud Messaging)** | Push notifications when a new alert drops, even if the app is killed. **This is critical for a 40–50 alerts/day fire response app** — chasers need to be woken up. |
| **Firebase Storage** | Doc attachments, signature images, audit logs. |
| **Firebase Admin (in Next.js API routes)** | Server-side user mgmt, FCM sends, privileged ops. |

What I'd **add or swap**, surgically:

- **Firestore → Postgres** *only* if you outgrow it or want SQL analytics. The "10% of FDs not broadcasting unencrypted" + trend analysis you described is way easier in Postgres + Metabase/PostgREST than querying Firestore. But this is a future migration, not a day-one rebuild.
- **Custom API server (Node/Fastify or Python/FastAPI)** in front of the DB for the CMS, homeowner lookup orchestration, Twilio outbound calls, and the FD-coverage analytics. Firebase Functions can do some of this but you'll outgrow it.
- **A real-time layer** — Firestore's real-time listeners are already there. If you swap to Postgres, add Supabase Realtime or a Socket.io server. Don't reinvent.
- **Skip-tracing API** for homeowner lookup — TLO, Batch, REISkip, or TruePeopleSearch scraper. This is the missing link for the "create contact from address" CMS flow.
- **Twilio** for the automated SMS + voice + voicemail drops to homeowners.
- **Resend or SendGrid** for the email side.
- **Mapbox or Google Maps** for the geocoding + distance + directions (you already use Google Maps in the screenshots).

## React Native vs Flutter — same answer, stronger reasoning

Given the **scope just exploded from "personal capture app" to "commercial US-wide SaaS"**, this decision is bigger now. Recommendation unchanged: **React Native**, and here's why it matters more:

| | **React Native (Expo)** | **Flutter** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Code reuse from current Next.js | **~70%** of business logic, types, hooks, validation, API client, state — all port as-is | **~5%** — every line in Dart, two codebases forever |
| Team ramp-up if you hire | Any React dev is productive on day 1 | Learn Dart + Flutter framework |
| Web PWA stays alive | `react-native-web` keeps one codebase serving web, iOS, Android | Flutter web is heavier and visually distinct |
| iOS rollout | Expo + EAS Build handles signing, TestFlight, App Store in one workflow | Same but a second toolchain |
| Chaser vs Supe app split | One Expo project, two entry points (`chaser`, `supe`), shared packages | Same — but you're maintaining Dart code twice |
| Native modules (FCM, location, geofencing, signature pad) | All mature, official `@react-native-firebase/*` packages | All available, slightly more verbose |

If you go React Native with Expo, the chaser app and supe app are **one project, two entry points** — they share the auth flow, the alert model, the chat, the geocoding, the storage layer, the design tokens. Only the navigation, visible features, and role-gated screens differ. That's huge.

**The conversion path I'd actually run on this monorepo:**

1. Promote `apps/android` from placeholder to a real Expo prebuild project — or keep native if you want full Android control (signature pad, FCM background handlers, geofencing). Expo is faster to ship; bare RN is more flexible.
2. Move all `apps/web/src/lib/*` shared logic (alerts model, auth context, FCM helper, API client, validation) into `packages/shared/` and import it from the RN app.
3. Migrate screens in this order: **Incidents list → Incident details → Profile/Signature → Chat → Contacts → Chasers map**. The web PWA stays live the whole time.
4. For the Supe app features (close incident, view all chasers, supe-to-supe chat), add a role-based navigation split.

## Your specific business features → how they map

| Feature | Where it lives |
| --- | --- |
| Live alert feed (home page) | Firestore real-time listener on `alerts/` collection, React Native `FlatList` with FlashList for perf |
| Geocode + distance + directions | Geocode on server (Mapbox or Google), cache lat/lng on the alert doc, distance computed client-side from chaser location |
| FD coverage analytics (which 10% don't broadcast, which only send first dispatch unencrypted) | New `fd_coverage` table in Postgres, populated by ingestion script that diffs BNN notification patterns; CMS dashboard reads from it |
| CMS back office (create contact from address) | New `apps/cms` Next.js app, or admin routes in the existing `apps/web` |
| Skip-trace homeowner lookup | Server-side API route → TLO/Batch, populate `homeowner` record on the alert |
| Automated SMS + voice + email | Twilio (Programmable Messaging + Voice) + Resend, triggered by alert status changes |
| Chat (Chaser→Supe = group; Supe↔Supe = 1:1; Chaser↔Chaser = 1:1) | Firestore `chats/` collection with a `participants` array + `visibility` rule enforced by security rules. Single thread per chaser-supe conversation. |
| Chaser location visible to supe app, but not to other chasers | FCM location topic + Firestore `users/{uid}/location` with security rules: `read` allowed if requester.role == 'supe' |
| Supe location visible to all supes | Same pattern, role-gated |
| Push when new alert drops | FCM topic subscribe per county/region, or per-user with payload |
| Marketing site + SEO + employee management | `apps/web` (existing) + new `apps/marketing` if you want separation; both on Vercel |
| Your personal BNN capture (notification-database app) | Stays separate, sends to the cloud backend (custom API mode in the existing app) |

## AI tools to drive the conversion on this specific repo

Given the size of `nfa-alerts-enterprise`, I'd use:

| Tool | Job |
| --- | --- |
| **Cursor** with the `nfa-alerts-enterprise` repo indexed | Day-to-day: ask "convert this Next.js screen to a React Native screen that uses the same data hook", accept the diff |
| **Claude Code / me, with codebase access** | Architecture mapping — the big "what becomes what" doc, the security rules rewrite, the Firestore schema review |
| **v0.dev** | Generate the new screen layouts in shadcn/Tailwind first, then port to React Native Paper / NativeBase |
| **bolt.new** | Scaffold the Expo project shell with the chaser + supe entry points |
| **DhiWise** | Has actual Next.js → React Native migration if you want a head start |
| **CodeRabbit / Sourcery** | PR review on the conversion PRs to catch regressions |

The realistic workflow: **I'll read the nfa-alerts-enterprise repo end-to-end, produce a per-file migration map, then we go screen-by-screen with Cursor accelerating the boilerplate and me handling the architecture and security rules.**

## What I noticed in the screenshots

Quick observations that affect the rebuild:

- **Chaser app bottom nav has "Notifications" twice** (1st and 4th tab both labeled "Notifications"). That's a bug — the 4th should be Profile or similar. Worth fixing in the rebuild.
- **Supe app nav** is `Notifications / Chasers / Chat / Supe` — clean. Keep that structure.
- **Incident details tabs** (Details / Homeowner / Docs / Sign) is good UX. Sign tab is for the on-site homeowner sign-off; signature on Profile is for the employee. Two different uses, keep both.
- **Profile has Push Notifications, Location Tracking, Geofence Alerts** — all three need first-class toggles in the RN rebuild with proper FCM topic + location permission flows.
- **Live Weather card** on incident details — needs a weather API (Open-Meteo is free, no key needed).
- **Map** is Google Maps embedded — fine, or swap to Mapbox for cost.
- **INC + FD IDs** are the join keys for your FD coverage analytics. Make sure the schema preserves them as separate fields, not concatenated.

## Values You Must Provide

Before I can plan the conversion concretely, I need:

| What | Why | Format |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sanity-check the architecture above** — agree that the commercial app stays cloud-backed and your home PC is just a viewer? | Don't want to plan around the wrong topology. | Yes / no / push back |

| **App store accounts** — do you have Apple Developer + Google Play developer accounts set up? | Blocks the actual submission. | Yes/no for each |
| **Budget / scale targets** — how many chasers/supes are you onboarding over the next 6 months? | Affects whether Firestore is enough or you need to move to Postgres. | Number range |

And treating the data as the product (not the app) is the right call — the app is one delivery channel, the county-scoped alert feed is the actual product you sell. Let me lay out the concrete plan.

## Step 0: Freeze nfa-alerts-v2 immediately

This is the most important thing I'm going to say. **Stop touching v2 today.** Before any other work:

```powershell
# From D:\github\nfa-alerts-v2
git status
git log --oneline -20
git tag v2-FROZEN-2026-07-20
git checkout -b v2-frozen-snapshot
git push origin v2-frozen-snapshot
```

Then **don't `git pull` on v2, don't `npm install` on it, don't open it in Cursor unless you're reading**. From this point forward, **the rebuild lives in `nfa-alerts-enterprise`** — that's the source of truth. When enterprise is stable, v2 gets deprecated and replaced.

The reason: if you've been making changes you can't fully account for, every change you make from here is building on a foundation you don't trust. Worse, you said you may have accidentally edited v2 while thinking you were in enterprise — that's a recipe for losing the live app. Freeze, audit, move on.

Quick audit you can do this week to know how bad it is:
```powershell
git log --since="6 months ago" --stat
git diff main..HEAD --name-only  # see what's actually changed
```

If the diff is small, carry those changes into enterprise. If it's big, treat v2-frozen-snapshot as the recoverable artifact and rebuild fresh in enterprise.

## The new architecture — concrete

```
[4axe.com]               ← marketing site, public, SEO (Next.js static)
[4axe.com/app]           ← web app login (Next.js PWA, Firebase Auth)
[4axe.com/admin]         ← CMS (Next.js admin, role-gated)
[future: chaser.apk]     ← React Native, Expo
[future: supe.apk]       ← React Native, Expo (same project, role-gated entry)

              ↓ all HTTPS, all auth-gated

[API layer]
  - Next.js API routes for web (auth, CRUD, simple ops)
  - Optional: standalone Fastify/Express service for heavy work
    (Twilio orchestration, skip-trace, ingestion from phone)

              ↓

[Postgres on your PC, drives mounted]
  - single database: nfa_alerts
  - schema-per-domain (not schema-as-tenant — use company_id)
  - partitioned tables for high-volume data
  - automated backups to Backblaze B2 or S3

              ↑

[Phone-to-PC ingest]
  - Tailscale mesh on phone + PC (already on your radar)
  - Capture app POSTs to https://<pc-tailscale-hostname>/api/ingest
  - Or: Tailscale Funnel for public ingress with token auth
  - Fallback: Cloudflare Tunnel to the same endpoint

[Docker Compose on your PC]
  - postgres
  - redis (queue, cache, pubsub)
  - api (the heavy server)
  - caddy (reverse proxy + TLS for Tailscale Funnel)
  - backup (cron to B2/S3)
```

**Why Tailscale, not just direct LAN access:** Tailscale gives you a stable hostname (`tony-pc.tail-net.ts.net`) that works whether you're on your home Wi-Fi or LTE. The phone doesn't need to know your home IP. Tailscale Funnel is the escape hatch for when you want a public URL without opening ports on your router. This is the standard "homelab meets production" pattern.

**Why Docker:** You said "has to be in a container to ship." Right call. When you onboard a customer who wants self-hosted, you ship them a `docker-compose.yml` that brings up the whole stack. Dev/prod parity, no "works on my machine."

## Data model — Postgres schema sketch

For 20K+ rows/day with multi-tenancy, the design choices that matter:

```sql
-- Tenancy
companies (
  id uuid pk,
  name text,
  plan text,                    -- 'starter' | 'pro' | 'enterprise'
  assigned_counties text[],     -- e.g. '{"monmouth","ocean","middlesex"}' NJ
  created_at timestamptz,
  status text                   -- 'active' | 'paused' | 'cancelled'
)

users (
  id uuid pk,
  company_id uuid fk -> companies.id,  -- every user belongs to exactly one company
  email citext unique,
  phone e164,
  role text,                    -- 'admin' | 'supe' | 'chaser'
  fcm_token text,                -- for push
  last_location geography,       -- PostGIS, for supe map
  last_location_at timestamptz,
  status text,                   -- 'active' | 'off_duty'
  created_at timestamptz
)

-- Counties (reference data, seeded once)
counties (
  id serial pk,
  state char(2),
  name text,
  fips_code char(5) unique,
  geometry geography(MultiPolygon)  -- PostGIS for point-in-polygon assignment
)

-- Alerts — partitioned by month
alerts (
  id uuid pk,
  company_id uuid fk,
  external_id text,              -- INC-003842 from BNN
  fire_dept_id text,             -- FD: qn4632 — critical for your coverage analytics
  type text,                     -- 'fire' | 'medical' | 'other'
  severity text,                 -- '1st alarm' | '2nd alarm' | 'all hands' | etc.
  address_raw text,
  address_parsed jsonb,          -- {street, city, state, zip}
  location geography(Point, 4326),
  county_id int fk,
  status text,                   -- 'active' | 'closed' | 'cancelled'
  reported_at timestamptz,
  closed_at timestamptz,
  primary key (id, reported_at)  -- composite for partitioning
) partition by range (reported_at);

-- Monthly partitions created by a cron job / pg_partman
-- alerts_2026_07, alerts_2026_08, ...

-- Alert updates — append-only, this is where the 20x multiplier comes from
alert_updates (
  id bigserial,
  alert_id uuid,
  sequence int,                  -- 0 = initial, 1+ = updates in order
  payload jsonb,                 -- the raw notification body
  parsed jsonb,                  -- the structured extraction
  received_at timestamptz default now(),
  primary key (id, received_at)
) partition by range (received_at);

-- FD coverage analytics
fire_departments (
  id text pk,                    -- 'qn4632'
  name text,
  county_id int fk,
  broadcast_mode text,           -- 'unencrypted' | 'encrypted' | 'mixed'
  first_dispatch_only bool,      -- true if they only send first dispatch unencrypted
  last_verified_at timestamptz,
  notes text
)

-- Homeowner contacts (CMS output)
contacts (
  id uuid pk,
  company_id uuid,
  alert_id uuid fk,
  name text,
  phone e164,
  email citext,
  property_address text,
  skip_trace_source text,        -- 'tlo' | 'batch' | 'manual'
  skip_trace_data jsonb,
  created_at timestamptz
)

-- Outbound comms log
contact_attempts (
  id bigserial,
  contact_id uuid,
  channel text,                  -- 'sms' | 'voice' | 'email'
  twilio_sid text,
  status text,                   -- 'queued' | 'delivered' | 'failed' | 'no-answer'
  payload jsonb,
  attempted_at timestamptz
)

-- Chat (kept for migration from Firestore)
chat_threads (
  id uuid pk,
  company_id uuid,
  participants uuid[],
  thread_type text,              -- '1on1' | 'chaser_to_supe_group' | 'supe_to_supe'
  visible_to uuid[],             -- who can see this thread (enforces the "only the originating chaser sees the group message" rule)
  last_message_at timestamptz
)

chat_messages (
  id bigserial,
  thread_id uuid,
  sender_id uuid,
  body text,
  sent_at timestamptz default now(),
  read_by uuid[]
)
```

**Key design choices:**

- **`company_id` on every table, no exceptions.** Every query goes through a middleware that injects `WHERE company_id = $current`. PostgREST or a query builder can enforce this. This is what makes multi-tenancy work.
- **Partitioning on `alerts` and `alert_updates` by month.** When a customer is on the plan for 3 years and you have 50 customers, you don't want to query 5 years of data. Old partitions get compressed and moved to cold storage transparently. `pg_partman` automates this.
- **PostGIS for geography.** Point-in-polygon assignment (which county does an alert belong to) becomes a single query, not a lookup table. Lets you also compute distance from chaser to alert using the `ST_Distance` function. Way faster than haversine in app code.
- **`visible_to` array on `chat_threads`** enforces your specific chat rule: chaser A messages supe B → thread is visible to {chaser_A, all_supes_in_company}. When supe B responds, the message is in that thread, visible to {chaser_A, all_supes_in_company}. When supe C also responds, same thread. Chaser D never sees it.
- **No Firebase for the data layer going forward.** Postgres is the source of truth. Firebase can stay for Auth + FCM only, which are the things it's genuinely good at.

| Volume | Firestore | Postgres local |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 500 alerts/day × 10 updates = 5K rows/day = ~1.8M rows/year | At 2KB/row = 3.6GB/year just for alert data | Same data on your drives = ~$0/year |
| 10 customers × 5 years | ~180GB stored, ~$32/month just for storage, plus reads/writes | A single 4TB drive = $80 one-time |
| Real-time listener reads (chasing app refreshes every 30s) | $0.06 per 100K reads, easily 5–10M reads/day for 100 active chasers = $3–6/day = $100–200/month | Local reads = free |
| **Year 1 estimate, 10 customers** | **~$1,500–2,500/month** | **~$0/month + $80 hardware** |

The math is obvious. Your instinct is right.

## 1. High-Level System Purpose

**National Fire Alerts (NFA)** is an emergency response coordination platform connecting supervisors (Supes) with field responders (Chasers) for organizations like Miami-Dade Fire Rescue.

**Core Capabilities:**
- Real-time incident management and alerting
- Role-based communication (Chaser ↔ Supe chat)
- Document workflow (capture, sign, PDF generation)
- Location tracking for field responders
- Push notifications for incident updates
- Mobile-first PWA (max 448px viewport)

**Responsibility:** Manages user authentication, profile lifecycle, role-based access, and device fingerprinting for ban enforcement.

# Product Context

## Problem Statement

Emergency response organizations need efficient coordination between field responders and supervisors during incidents. Traditional communication methods (radio, phone) lack:
- Real-time location visibility
- Document capture and signing workflows
- Incident history and audit trails
- Efficient route planning for multiple incidents

## Solution

NFA Alerts provides a unified platform where:
- **Supes** dispatch and monitor Chasers in real-time
- **Chasers** receive incident alerts, respond, and document their work
- **Everyone** communicates through secure, role-based chat
- **Documents** are captured, signed, and stored digitally

## User Journeys

### Chaser Flow
1. Receive push notification for new incident
2. View incident details (address, type, alarm level)
3. Respond to incident (adds to their active incidents)
4. Navigate using route planner
5. On-site: capture photos, collect homeowner info
6. Get homeowner signature + sign themselves
7. Generate signed document PDF

### Supe Flow
1. Monitor all active incidents and chaser locations
2. View real-time chaser status (Responding/Available/Offline)
3. Communicate with chasers via chat
4. Award "Secured" status when chaser wins homeowner
5. Remove responders or close incidents as needed

### Admin Flow
1. Manage user accounts (approve, suspend, ban)
2. Configure locations/regions
3. View system-wide activity

## Key Differentiators
- **Mobile-first PWA** - Works like native app without app store
- **Real-time everything** - Incidents, chat, presence updates instantly
- **Digital document workflow** - No paper, immediate PDF generation
- **Role-based intelligence** - UI adapts to user role
- **Interactive onboarding** - Guided walkthrough for new users

# Subscription Architecture Plan

Subscription logic is intentionally out of scope for the monorepo migration.

## Status

- No subscription logic was added during migration.
- No billing provider was selected during migration.
- No entitlement checks were added during migration.

## Future Planning Principles

- Keep emergency-response realtime behavior independent from billing-provider availability.
- Centralize account, tenant, entitlement, and audit contracts before implementing paid plans.
- Treat billing webhooks as backend-only routes with explicit verification and replay protection.
- Do not couple Android or iOS clients directly to billing webhooks.

A dedicated subscription architecture task should define tenant model, billing source of truth, entitlement cache, failure modes, audit logging, and production rollout controls before implementation.

# Project Brief

## Overview

**National Fire Alerts (NFA)** - Emergency response coordination platform connecting supervisors (Supes) with field responders (Chasers) for organizations like Miami-Dade Fire Rescue.

## Core Requirements

### Business Goals
- Real-time incident management and coordination
- Location tracking for field responders
- Secure communication between Supes and Chasers
- Document management and digital signing
- Push notifications for new incidents

### User Roles
| Role | Responsibilities |
|------|------------------|
| **Chaser** | View/respond to incidents, chat with supes, upload documents |

1. **Incident Management** - CRUD, filtering, favorites/bookmarks, hide/mute

4. **Route Planning** - Nearest-neighbor algorithm for responded incidents
5. **Push Notifications** - Web push for new incidents and messages

## Next.js PWA Guidance (from Context7 — Next.js official docs, 2026)

### Recommended manifest approach
Next.js App Router supports a native `manifest.ts` in the app directory (Route Handler pattern) for dynamic manifests. The current static `apps/web/public/manifest.json` is valid and functional but the official recommendation is `apps/web/src/app/manifest.ts`:

```typescript
// apps/web/src/app/manifest.ts
import type { MetadataRoute } from 'next'

export default function manifest(): MetadataRoute.Manifest {
  return {
    name: 'NFA Alerts - Emergency Response Platform',
    short_name: 'NFA Alerts',
    start_url: '/',
    display: 'standalone',
    // ...
  }
}
```

**Current repo uses**: `apps/web/public/manifest.json` (static). Works but less flexible for dynamic theming.

### Recommended service worker security headers
Official Next.js PWA guide recommends explicit security headers in `apps/web/next.config.ts` for service workers:

```javascript
// apps/web/next.config.ts
async headers() {
  return [
    { source: '/sw.js', headers: [
      { key: 'Cache-Control', value: 'no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate' },
      { key: 'Content-Type', value: 'application/javascript; charset=utf-8' },
    ]},
  ]
}
```

**Current repo**: No explicit SW headers in `apps/web/next.config.ts`. Risk: browser may cache a stale service worker.

### Dual service worker concern
The current app registers both `/sw.js` and `/firebase-messaging-sw.js`. The official guide uses a single service worker. Firebase's own guidance supports a separate messaging service worker, so the dual pattern is intentional — but the SW scope and cache-control headers should be verified to avoid conflicts.

# Security, Secrets, and Subscription Architecture

Last updated: 2026-05-18

This plan defines the commercial security, secrets, tenant, billing, and entitlement architecture for NFA Alerts. It is documentation-only and does not authorize Firebase deploys, production data mutation, Android UI/business logic changes, real secret insertion, `google-services.json` commits, commits, or pushes.

This document expands the placeholder planning principles in `docs/commercial/SUBSCRIPTION_ARCHITECTURE_PLAN.md`. If both documents disagree later, this document is the more specific commercial architecture plan.

## Repo Evidence Used

- Production Firebase project is currently documented as `nfa-alerts-v2`.
- The web/PWA lives in `apps/web` and owns Next.js API routes.
- Firebase CLI config, Firestore rules, indexes, and storage rules live in `firebase/`.
- Server-side Firebase Admin initialization currently loads credentials only from environment-provided values.
- Existing roles are `chaser`, `supe`, and `admin` on `profiles/{uid}.role`.
- Existing Firestore rules are single-tenant and profile-role based; they do not yet model tenant memberships or billing entitlements.
- Android package is `com.emergency.alerts`; Android consumes normalized Firestore docs and must not parse raw alerts or call `POST /api/webhook`.
- No Stripe, Google Play Billing, commercial tenant, subscription, or entitlement implementation was found in active source.

## Recommended Architecture

NFA Alerts should use a trusted-backend entitlement architecture:

1. Clients authenticate with Firebase Auth.
2. Web/PWA users start Stripe Checkout or open Stripe Customer Portal through Next.js backend routes.
3. Android users purchase through Google Play Billing on-device, then send purchase tokens to a backend verification route.
4. Stripe webhooks and Google Play verification/notification events are processed by backend-only code using server secrets from Google Cloud Secret Manager.
5. Backend writes normalized subscription and entitlement state into Firestore.
6. Web and Android clients read Firestore entitlements and tenant memberships; they never trust billing client state as the source of truth.
7. Firestore rules enforce tenant membership, role, and entitlement gates for protected data.

Firestore remains the realtime operational database. Billing provider availability must not block emergency incident rendering for already-authorized users; entitlement outages should fail closed for admin/billing actions and fail with a documented grace policy for time-critical responder workflows.

## Secret Manager Strategy

Google Cloud Secret Manager should be the source of truth for backend secrets in Google-hosted environments. Runtime code should consume secrets through platform-supported injection or Application Default Credentials wherever possible; local development should use empty `.env.example` placeholders and operator-managed local secrets outside git.

Principles:

- Store one logical secret per Secret Manager secret name, using environment-specific projects or prefixes.
- Grant `Secret Manager Secret Accessor` only to the runtime service account that needs a secret.
- Prefer Application Default Credentials and workload identity over checked-in service account key files.
- Rotate secret versions without renaming environment variables.
- Disable or destroy old secret versions only after the new version is deployed and verified.
- Audit access logs and alert on unexpected secret access.
- Never print secret values in logs, docs, tests, terminal output, screenshots, or bug reports.
- Do not commit `.env*` except `.env.example` with empty assignments only.
- Do not commit Firebase service account JSON, Google Play service account JSON, Stripe keys, webhook secrets, Android signing keys, or `google-services.json`.

Recommended naming:

- Secret Manager secret names should match runtime environment variable names where possible.
- Production and staging should be separated by Google Cloud project, deployment environment, or explicit prefix such as `PROD_` and `STAGING_`.
- Public client configuration values may remain normal environment configuration, but no values belong in repo docs.

## Android Client Secret Boundary

Android must not hold backend secrets. The Android app may include Firebase client configuration from local `apps/android/app/google-services.json` and Play Billing product identifiers, but it must never include:

- `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`
- `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`
- `GOOGLE_PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON`
- `FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON`
- `FIREBASE_PRIVATE_KEY`
- `WEBHOOK_AUTH_TOKEN`
- OpenAI keys, server Google Maps/geocoding keys, or backend signing secrets

Android must not call `POST /api/webhook`, admin maintenance routes, Stripe webhooks, or backend-only billing webhooks. Android should call only explicitly designed, authenticated, App Check-protected client API routes such as purchase verification or entitlement refresh.

Android purchase state is not authoritative. The app can display local Play Billing status optimistically, but access decisions must come from Firestore entitlements written by the trusted backend after server-side verification.

## App Check and Play Integrity Rollout

App Check should protect Firebase products and custom backend APIs from non-genuine clients. For Android, use the Play Integrity provider for release builds and a debug provider only for local development.

Rollout phases:

1. Register Android app SHA-256 fingerprints and configure the Play Integrity provider.
2. Add App Check initialization before Firebase SDK use in Android.
3. Add App Check token forwarding to client-owned backend routes.

**On every alert (Layer 3, async):**

- If no alert received in expected window, flag as "coverage gap"
- Update FD reputation score: response time × frequency × severity mix
- Detect when an FD changes from unencrypted to encrypted (alerts stop arriving)
- Cross-reference weather, topography, time of day to predict alert volume

**For the dispatcher (the supe app):**
- AI suggests which chaser to dispatch based on distance, current load, history
- Auto-generate a daily brief: "FD qn4632 is 15% slower this week than last"
- "Coverage gap alert: county X has received 0 alerts in the last 4 hours, expected 3"

**For the homeowner (Layer 2 outbound):**
- Voice AI that knows it's a fire at their address, gives them what to do, asks if they're OK
- Hands off to a human chaser/supervisor if needed (warm transfer)
- Sends them a packet: insurance claim info, Red Cross contact, FEMA info, contractor referrals

## The visualization angle — why animation matters here

The current app uses static maps and list views. For a real-time emergency response product, the **map is the dashboard**. Modern data viz tech that elevates this:

| Tech | What it does for you |
| --- | --- |
| **Mapbox GL JS** | Smoother pan/zoom than Google, custom layers, vector tiles |
| **Deck.gl** | GPU-accelerated data viz on top of Mapbox — heatmaps, scatterplots, 3D extrusions, animated arcs |
| **Observable Plot** | Fast, composable charts for the analytics dashboards in the CMS |
| **D3** | For the bespoke "FD coverage map" with the colored regions |
| **Framer Motion + React Spring** | Smooth in-app animations for the alert list, transition between alerts, slide-in for new incidents |
| **Three.js** (optional) | 3D topographic visualization of alert density by elevation, terrain, building density |
| **Mapbox + custom shaders** | Animated "pulse" overlay on the alert location when it first comes in |

Concrete UX upgrade ideas:

- **Live alert feed** becomes an **animated map** as the default home view. List is a secondary view for triage.
- **Each new alert** drops in as a **pulsing red dot** that expands and fades, with a small label that auto-arranges to not overlap other alerts.
- **Chaser positions** are small colored dots, color-coded by status (responding, available, off-duty).
- **Coverage gap zones** are shaded overlays that update as data comes in — counties that are "behind" on expected alert volume get a faint orange tint that intensifies.
- **FD reputation** is a stacked bar chart on the analytics dashboard that animates as new data lands.
- **The homeowner's view** (if you build a public-facing one) is a single beautiful page with: "Emergency response is on the way. Here's what to do. Here's who's coming."

## The data product angle

The CSVs you have are the seed. Once the system has been running for 6+ months, the database contains:

- Every alert in your covered counties with type, severity, time, FD, response
- Every homeowner's contact info (where skip-trace succeeded)
- Every outreach attempt and outcome
- Every chaser's response time per alert
- Every FD's broadcast pattern (encrypted/unencrypted, first-dispatch-only, etc.)

**You can sell this as:**

| Product | Customer | Price model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Real-time fire alert feed (per county)** | Insurance carriers, property mgmt companies, alarm companies | Per-county subscription, monthly |
| **Coverage gap reports** | Municipalities, fire departments, emergency mgmt agencies | Per-county annual license |
| **Response reputation data** | Insurance underwriting, ratings agencies | Per-query API or annual subscription |
| **Homeowner outreach automation** | Restoration companies, public adjusters | Per-attempt fee |
| **Aggregated market intelligence** | Investors, industry analysts, journalists | Custom contract |

You don't have to build all of these on day one. But the data model needs to support them so you're not re-platforming in 18 months.

# EMU — Emergency Management Unit

**Canonical product name:** EMU (was: nfa-alerts, nfa-alerts-v2, nfa-alerts-enterprise, emu-incidents)

A commercial, multi-tenant, real-time fire-alert coordination platform.
Chasers (field responders) and Supes (supervisors) receive household fire alerts
the moment they hit unencrypted dispatch channels, with geocoded addresses,
distance, directions, role-based chat, and automated homeowner outreach.

## Why this repo exists

This is the canonical rebuild. Earlier names and copies existed under
`nfa-alerts-*`, `emu-alerts-*`, `emu-incidents`, `EMU_*`. They are all folded
into this repo. The Firebase project is `emu-incidents` (now also aliased as
`nfa-alerts-v2`). The marketing site is **4axe.com**. The Tailscale node that
runs the API is `chaoscentral` (PC) and the capture device is `anthonys-s26-ultra`
(phone).

## Architecture (Phase 0 — live data first)

```
[ BNN notification ]  ->  [ Android phone (anthonys-s26-ultra) ]
                              |  nfa-alerts-v2 app or notification-database
                              |  POST application/json
                              v
                       [ Tailscale mesh ]
                              |
                              v
                       [ PC ingest service : chaoscentral.tailb71e7e.ts.net:8787 ]
                              |  Fastify + Zod
                              |  validates, normalizes, geocodes, persists
                              v
                       [ PostgreSQL 18 + pgvector ]  <-- the canonical store
                              ^
                              |
                       [ Next.js web app (4axe.com) ]
                              |  reads via Drizzle ORM
                              v
                       [ React Native (later) ] -- chaser / supe apps
```

## Repo layout

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `apps/emu-ingest/` | The Fastify ingest service that receives notifications from the phone and writes to Postgres |
| `db/migrations/` | SQL migration files, run in order |
| `db/seeds/` | Reference data (fire departments, counties) — CSVs imported by `scripts/import_fire_depts.mjs` |
| `docs/` | Architecture, operations, ADRs |
| `scripts/` | Importers, ops helpers |
| `deploy/` | Docker Compose, Tailscale / Cloudflare Tunnel configs |

## First 7 days — what's already in motion

1. **Day 0** (today): this bootstrap. Ingest service skeleton + schema migrations.
2. **Day 1**: end-to-end test — phone → PC → Postgres, one row visible.
3. **Day 2**: import the Fire Depts master CSV (27,803 departments) + NJ encryption verification.
4. **Day 3**: first coverage-gap query — "which NJ FDs we expect to hear from but didn't."

6. **Day 6-7**: first CMS module — company admin + user admin.

-- 0001_init.sql
-- EMU core schema: alerts, alert_updates, fire_departments, contacts, contact_attempts
-- Postgres 18 + PostGIS + pgvector
-- Multi-tenant: every business table has company_id
-- Run order: 0001 -> 0002 -> ... -> 9999

BEGIN;

-- ============================================================
-- Extensions
-- ============================================================
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "uuid-ossp";
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "pgcrypto";
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

-- ============================================================
-- Reference data: counties (seeded once)
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE counties (
    id           SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    state        CHAR(2) NOT NULL,
    name         TEXT NOT NULL,
    fips_code    CHAR(5) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    geometry     GEOMETRY(MultiPolygon, 4326),
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_counties_state ON counties(state);
CREATE INDEX idx_counties_geom ON counties USING GIST(geometry);

-- ============================================================
-- Fire departments (seeded from master_fire_directory.csv)
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE fire_departments (
    id                            UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    fdid                          TEXT,
    state                         CHAR(2) NOT NULL,
    county                        TEXT,
    city                          TEXT,
    department_name               TEXT NOT NULL,
    department_key                TEXT UNIQUE,
    volunteer_yes_no              TEXT,
    first_dispatch_encrypted      TEXT,
    remaining_dispatches_encrypted TEXT,
    channel_info                  TEXT,
    signal_type                   TEXT,
    encryption_type               TEXT,
    policy_requires_encryption    TEXT,
    population_served             INTEGER,
    active_career                 INTEGER,
    active_volunteer              INTEGER,
    active_paid_per_call          INTEGER,
    hq_address                    TEXT,
    hq_city                       TEXT,
    hq_state                      CHAR(2),
    hq_zip                        TEXT,
    hq_phone                      TEXT,
    hq_fax                        TEXT,
    website                       TEXT,
    dept_type                     TEXT,
    organization_type             TEXT,
    stations                      INTEGER,
    notes                         TEXT,
    policy_sources                TEXT,
    last_updated                  TIMESTAMPTZ,
    embedding                     VECTOR(384),  -- pgvector for fuzzy FD matching
    created_at                    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at                    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_fire_departments_state ON fire_departments(state);
CREATE INDEX idx_fire_departments_county ON fire_departments(state, county);
CREATE INDEX idx_fire_departments_encryption ON fire_departments(encryption_type);
CREATE INDEX idx_fire_departments_first_dispatch_enc ON fire_departments(first_dispatch_encrypted);
CREATE INDEX idx_fire_departments_remaining_dispatch_enc ON fire_departments(remaining_dispatches_encrypted);
CREATE INDEX idx_fire_departments_dept_key ON fire_departments(department_key);
-- HNSW index for fast approximate nearest neighbor on embeddings
CREATE INDEX idx_fire_departments_embedding ON fire_departments USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

-- ============================================================
-- Tenancy
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE companies (
    id                UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    name              TEXT NOT NULL,
    slug              TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    plan              TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'starter',  -- 'starter' | 'pro' | 'enterprise'
    assigned_counties TEXT[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',     -- FIPS codes or county names
    status            TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',  -- 'active' | 'paused' | 'cancelled'
    contact_email     TEXT,
    contact_phone     TEXT,
    created_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE users (
    id                 UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    company_id         UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES companies(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    email              TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    phone              TEXT,
    display_name       TEXT,
    role               TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'chaser',  -- 'admin' | 'supe' | 'chaser'
    fcm_token          TEXT,
    last_location      GEOMETRY(Point, 4326),
    last_location_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
    status             TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',  -- 'active' | 'off_duty' | 'suspended'
    nickname           TEXT,
    created_at         TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at         TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_company ON users(company_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_role ON users(company_id, role);

-- ============================================================
-- Alerts — partitioned monthly on reported_at
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE alerts (
    id              UUID NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    company_id      UUID,                            -- nullable for raw ingest; assigned by ingestion
    external_id     TEXT,                            -- the INC-XXXXX from the source
    fire_dept_id    UUID REFERENCES fire_departments(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
    fire_dept_fdid  TEXT,                            -- raw FD ID from the alert text
    type            TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'fire',     -- 'fire' | 'medical' | 'other'
    severity        TEXT,                            -- '1st alarm' | '2nd alarm' | 'all hands' | ...
    address_raw     TEXT NOT NULL,
    address_parsed  JSONB,                           -- {street, city, state, zip}
    location        GEOMETRY(Point, 4326),
    county_id       INTEGER REFERENCES counties(id),
    state           CHAR(2),
    status          TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',   -- 'active' | 'closed' | 'cancelled'
    source          TEXT,                            -- 'bnn' | 'manual' | 'imported'
    raw_payload     JSONB,                           -- the full incoming notification body for forensics
    reported_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    closed_at       TIMESTAMPTZ,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    PRIMARY KEY (id, reported_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (reported_at);

CREATE INDEX idx_alerts_company ON alerts(company_id, reported_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_alerts_fire_dept ON alerts(fire_dept_id, reported_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_alerts_state ON alerts(state, reported_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_alerts_status ON alerts(status, reported_at DESC) WHERE status = 'active';
CREATE INDEX idx_alerts_location ON alerts USING GIST(location);

-- Default partition + first month partition
CREATE TABLE alerts_default PARTITION OF alerts DEFAULT;
CREATE TABLE alerts_2026_07 PARTITION OF alerts
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-07-01') TO ('2026-08-01');
CREATE TABLE alerts_2026_08 PARTITION OF alerts
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-08-01') TO ('2026-09-01');
CREATE TABLE alerts_2026_09 PARTITION OF alerts
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-09-01') TO ('2026-10-01');

-- ============================================================
-- Alert updates — append-only, this is the 20x volume multiplier
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE alert_updates (
    id           BIGSERIAL,
    alert_id     UUID NOT NULL,
    sequence     INTEGER NOT NULL,                   -- 0 = initial, 1+ = updates in order
    payload      JSONB NOT NULL,                     -- raw update text
    parsed       JSONB,                              -- structured extraction
    received_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    PRIMARY KEY (id, received_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (received_at);

CREATE INDEX idx_alert_updates_alert ON alert_updates(alert_id, sequence);
CREATE TABLE alert_updates_default PARTITION OF alert_updates DEFAULT;
CREATE TABLE alert_updates_2026_07 PARTITION OF alert_updates
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-07-01') TO ('2026-08-01');
CREATE TABLE alert_updates_2026_08 PARTITION OF alert_updates
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-08-01') TO ('2026-09-01');
CREATE TABLE alert_updates_2026_09 PARTITION OF alert_updates
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-09-01') TO ('2026-10-01');

-- ============================================================
-- Contacts (homeowner contact records created from alerts)
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE contacts (
    id                  UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    company_id          UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES companies(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    alert_id            UUID,
    name                TEXT,
    phone               TEXT,
    email               TEXT,
    property_address    TEXT,
    property_location   GEOMETRY(Point, 4326),
    skip_trace_source   TEXT,                         -- 'tlo' | 'batch' | 'manual'
    skip_trace_data     JSONB,
    embedding           VECTOR(384),                  -- for fuzzy match against new alerts
    created_at          TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at          TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_contacts_company ON contacts(company_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_contacts_alert ON contacts(alert_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_contacts_phone ON contacts(phone);
CREATE INDEX idx_contacts_email ON contacts(email);
CREATE INDEX idx_contacts_embedding ON contacts USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

-- ============================================================
-- Contact attempts (outreach log)
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE contact_attempts (
    id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    contact_id      UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES contacts(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    alert_id        UUID,
    channel         TEXT NOT NULL,                    -- 'sms' | 'voice' | 'email'
    direction       TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'outbound', -- 'outbound' | 'inbound'
    twilio_sid      TEXT,
    status          TEXT NOT NULL,                    -- 'queued' | 'delivered' | 'failed' | 'no-answer' | 'completed'
    duration_sec    INTEGER,
    payload         JSONB,
    attempted_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_contact_attempts_contact ON contact_attempts(contact_id, attempted_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_contact_attempts_alert ON contact_attempts(alert_id);

-- ============================================================
-- Ingest log (every notification that hits the service, dedup-aware)
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE ingest_log (
    id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    source          TEXT,                             -- 'bnn' | 'manual' | 'imported'
    received_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    alert_id        UUID,                             -- backfilled once dedup resolves
    raw_payload     JSONB NOT NULL,
    normalized      JSONB,                            -- the parsed structure
    dedup_key       TEXT,                             -- hash of external_id + reported_at + fd_id
    status          TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'received', -- 'received' | 'parsed' | 'deduped' | 'failed'
    error           TEXT
);
CREATE INDEX idx_ingest_log_received ON ingest_log(received_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_ingest_log_dedup ON ingest_log(dedup_key);
CREATE INDEX idx_ingest_log_alert ON ingest_log(alert_id);

-- ============================================================
-- Audit log (catches all writes for security review)
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE audit_log (
    id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    actor_id        UUID,                             -- user_id or 'system'
    action          TEXT NOT NULL,
    table_name      TEXT NOT NULL,
    row_id          UUID,
    before          JSONB,
    after           JSONB,
    occurred_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_audit_log_actor ON audit_log(actor_id, occurred_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_audit_log_table ON audit_log(table_name, occurred_at DESC);

-- ============================================================
-- Triggers: keep updated_at fresh
-- ============================================================
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION touch_updated_at()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN
    NEW.updated_at = NOW();
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_fire_departments_touch
    BEFORE UPDATE ON fire_departments
    FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();

CREATE TRIGGER trg_companies_touch
    BEFORE UPDATE ON companies
    FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();

CREATE TRIGGER trg_users_touch
    BEFORE UPDATE ON users
    FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();

CREATE TRIGGER trg_contacts_touch
    BEFORE UPDATE ON contacts
    FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();

COMMIT;

-- ============================================================
-- Convenience views
-- ============================================================

-- v_active_alerts: live alerts visible to a given company (assigned counties only)
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_active_alerts AS
SELECT
    a.id,
    a.external_id,
    a.fire_dept_id,
    fd.department_name AS fire_dept_name,
    a.type,
    a.severity,
    a.address_raw,
    a.location,
    c.name AS county_name,
    c.state AS county_state,
    a.status,
    a.reported_at,
    a.created_at
FROM alerts a
LEFT JOIN fire_departments fd ON fd.id = a.fire_dept_id
LEFT JOIN counties c ON c.id = a.county_id
WHERE a.status = 'active';

-- v_coverage_gaps: per FD, expected vs received alerts in last 24h
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_coverage_gaps_24h AS
SELECT
    fd.id AS fire_dept_id,
    fd.department_name,
    fd.state,
    fd.county,
    fd.first_dispatch_encrypted,
    fd.remaining_dispatches_encrypted,
    fd.encryption_type,
    -- Count alerts in last 24h from this FD
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM alerts a
     WHERE a.fire_dept_id = fd.id
       AND a.reported_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '24 hours') AS alerts_24h
FROM fire_departments fd
WHERE fd.encryption_type IN ('unencrypted', 'mixed');

DATABASE_URL=postgres://emu:emu@127.0.0.1:5432/emu

services:

# EMU Agent Contract

This is the canonical rebuild of the EMU (was: nfa-alerts, nfa-alerts-v2, nfa-alerts-enterprise, emu-incidents) product.

**Single source of truth: this repo at `D:\github\emu`.**

## What this repo is

A commercial, multi-tenant, real-time fire-alert coordination platform. Chasers and Supes get household fire alerts the moment they hit unencrypted dispatch channels, with geocoded addresses, distance, directions, role-based chat, and automated homeowner outreach. The data — not the app — is the product.

## Authority hierarchy

1. `AGENTS.md` (this file) — agent operating rules, what to do, what not to do
2. `README.md` — product overview, architecture diagram, dev quick start
3. `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` — system architecture, data model, deployment
4. `db/migrations/` — schema is the contract; migrations are append-only
5. `apps/emu-ingest/` — the ingest service; this is what the phone talks to
6. `scripts/` — importers, ops helpers
7. `deploy/docker-compose.yml` — the container spec

## What we are building (Phase 0 — get data flowing first)

| Order | What | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Bootstrap repo (this commit) | ✅ done |
| 2 | Postgres schema (alerts, alert_updates, fire_departments, contacts) | ✅ done |
| 3 | Fastify ingest service (POST /api/ingest) | ✅ done |
| 4 | CSV importer for Fire Depts master directory | ✅ done |
| 5 | Docker Compose for local Postgres | ✅ done |
| 6 | Postgres connection — needs operator action | ⏳ blocked |
| 7 | First end-to-end test: phone → ingest → Postgres | ⏳ pending |
| 8 | Import 27,803 fire departments | ⏳ pending |
| 9 | First coverage-gap query runs | ⏳ pending |
| 10 | Next.js web app (the existing 4axe.com PWA) gets pointed at this DB | ⏳ pending |

## Operating rules

- **Do not edit `db/migrations/0001_init.sql` after it ships.** Add new migrations with the next number.
- **Multi-tenant everything.** Every business table has `company_id`. No exceptions.
- **Bigger number is newer.** The `alerts` and `alert_updates` tables are partitioned monthly; new partitions are added by `scripts/ensure_partitions.mjs` (TODO).
- **Idempotent scripts.** Re-running the CSV importer updates existing rows, doesn't duplicate.
- **Bearer token on ingest.** `EMU_INGEST_TOKEN` is a 64-char hex string, generated once, shared only with the Android capture app. No token = reject the request.
- **Bifrost is the gate.** Any external tool/MCP that wants to touch Postgres goes through `agentcore-gateway`. Direct SQL from IDEs is forbidden by the master config.
- **No subscriptions where avoidable.** Use local AI / built-in tools first. Only add a paid service when the local option is provably insufficient.
- **No "remove the data."** Read-only on all historical CSV / JSON / Firebase exports. New work copies data into Postgres, never deletes the source.
